trial_name: EOLIA — Early VV-ECMO vs Conventional Ventilation in Severe ARDS (2018)
citation: Combes A, Hajage D, Capellier G, et al. Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(21):1965-1975.
one_liner: In very severe ARDS, early VV-ECMO did not significantly reduce 60-day mortality compared to conventional ventilation with rescue ECMO (35% vs 46%; RR 0.76; P=0.09), but high crossover and early stopping complicate interpretation.

pico.population: Adults with very severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 < 50 mmHg for >3h, <80 mmHg for >6h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO2 ≥60 mmHg for >6h) despite lung-protective ventilation.
pico.intervention: Early VV-ECMO (goal initiation within 2h) with ultra-protective ventilation (VT 3-4 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤24 cmH2O).
pico.comparison: Conventional lung-protective ventilation (Pplat 28-30 cmH2O) with protocolized escalation (prone positioning, NMBA) and rescue ECMO for refractory hypoxemia.

background.existing_knowledge: VV-ECMO was increasingly used as rescue support for refractory hypoxaemia/hypercapnia in ARDS, but contemporary randomised evidence was limited and confounded by centre effects, co-interventions, and evolving ventilatory standards.
background.knowledge_gap: Equipoise persisted about whether “early” ECMO (before multi-organ injury accrues) improves survival compared with an optimised conventional strategy that includes prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade, higher PEEP, and rescue options.
background.hypothesis: In adults with very severe ARDS, early initiation of VV-ECMO reduces 60-day mortality compared with conventional lung-protective ventilation with standardised escalation and the option of rescue ECMO.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, open-label, controlled, international trial with central randomisation (stratified by centre and by duration of mechanical ventilation before randomisation < 3 days vs ≥ 3 days) and a sequential (two-sided triangular) monitoring design.

inclusion: Adult ICU patients with ARDS and very severe respiratory failure despite low tidal-volume ventilation (target 6 mL/kg PBW) and PEEP ≥ 10 cmH2O, meeting at least one of: PaO2/FiO2 < 50 mmHg for > 3 h; PaO2/FiO2 < 80 mmHg for > 6 h; or pH < 7.25 with PaCO2 ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h despite RR increased to 35/min (maintaining Pplat ≤ 32 cmH2O).
exclusion: ≥ 7 days of mechanical ventilation before randomisation

methods.intervention: Early VV-ECMO (goal initiation within 2 h after randomisation) using percutaneous cannulation; anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin targeting aPTT 40–55 s (or anti-Xa 0.2–0.3 IU/mL). Post-cannulation “ultra-protective” ventilation targets: VT 3–4 mL/kg PBW; PEEP ≥ 10 cmH2O; Pplat ≤ 24 cmH2O; FiO2 0.30–0.60; RR 10–30/min.
methods.comparison: Conventional lung-protective ventilation, including higher-PEEP strategy (target Pplat 28–30 cmH2O) with strong encouragement to use neuromuscular blockade and prone positioning. Rescue therapies permitted (including inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin and recruitment manoeuvres); rescue ECMO allowed for refractory hypoxaemia (SaO2 < 80% for > 6 h despite recruitment manoeuvres, inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin, and prone positioning when feasible) and in the absence of irreversible multi-organ failure.
methods.blinding: Open-label; primary outcome (all-cause mortality) objective, but decisions around escalation and crossover were clinically mediated (with protocolised rescue criteria).
methods.sample_size_power: Assumed 60-day mortality 60% (control) vs 40% (ECMO) (absolute reduction 20%); α=0.05; power 80%; maximum sample size 331; interim analyses planned every 60 patients.
secondary_outcomes: Treatment failure by day 60 (death in ECMO group; death or crossover to ECMO in control)
Median days free from mechanical ventilation (inclusion to day 60)
Median days free from renal failure (inclusion to day 60)
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint at 60 days; additional follow-up through day 90 for mortality and selected secondary outcomes.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early for futility at 249 patients (331 planned).
60-day mortality was 35% (ECMO) vs 46% (control), RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.55–1.04, P=0.09).
28% of the control group crossed over to rescue ECMO.

outcomes_table.note: Frequentist primary endpoint did not cross prespecified significance boundary.
Key secondary endpoint; structurally penalises rescue ECMO crossover in control.
Between-group difference not statistically tested in the reported table.

outcomes_table.outcome: Median days free from mechanical ventilation (inclusion to day 60)
outcomes_table.note: Composite of survival and time off invasive ventilation; highly influenced by early deaths.

outcomes_table.outcome: Median days free from renal failure (inclusion to day 60)
outcomes_table.note: Supports a signal toward reduced multi-organ failure burden.
Co-intervention use was greater in control (as intended by protocolised escalation).
Clinically important harm signal consistent with ECMO anticoagulation and cannulation risks.
Potentially reflects circuit-related platelet consumption and/or anticoagulation effects.
Direction unexpected; small numbers; interpret cautiously.

safety: Bleeding leading to transfusion: 57/124 (46%) ECMO vs 35/125 (28%) control (difference 18%; 95% CI 6 to 30).
Severe thrombocytopenia: 34/124 (27%) ECMO vs 20/125 (16%) control (difference 12%; 95% CI 1 to 22).
Ischaemic stroke: 0/124 (0%) ECMO vs 6/125 (5%) control (difference −5%; 95% CI −10 to −2).

domains.notes: Central randomisation stratified by centre and pre-randomisation duration of mechanical ventilation (< 3 days vs ≥ 3 days), supporting allocation concealment and balance.
Open-label design; primary outcome objective. However, decisions to cross over to rescue ECMO (and timing) were clinically mediated, even with protocol criteria.
Primary analysis by intention-to-treat. 121/124 (97.6%) assigned to ECMO received ECMO; control “contamination” occurred via rescue crossover in 35/125 (28%).

Control received more prone positioning (90% vs 66%; difference −24%; 95% CI −35 to −14) and more inhaled vasodilators (62% vs 46%; difference −16%; 95% CI −29 to −3), which could reduce apparent incremental benefit of ECMO.
Groups were similar at enrolment (e.g., age 51.9 ± 12.5 vs 54.4 ± 13.4 years; SOFA 10.8 ± 3.4 vs 10.6 ± 3.3; PaO2/FiO2 73 ± 30 vs 72 ± 24 mmHg).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: randomisation and objective primary outcome support internal validity, but early stopping and substantial rescue ECMO crossover plausibly diluted mortality differences and complicate interpretation of effect size.

domains.notes: The cohort represents a highly selected, very severe ARDS population (PaO2/FiO2 ~72 mmHg) meeting strict physiological thresholds; patients ventilated ≥ 7 days, those with BMI > 45, pregnancy, and those with major contraindications were excluded. Of 1015 eligible patients, 249 were randomised, implying substantial screening/selection.

Implementation requires mature ECMO programmes (and, in this trial, a mobile ECMO retrieval model for non-ECMO centres), limiting immediate generalisability to low-volume or resource-limited settings. Most applicable to high-income ICUs that can deliver contemporary lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, and timely VV-ECMO with complication management.

external_validity.verdict: Good for patients with very severe ARDS in experienced ECMO networks; limited for broader ARDS populations and health systems without rapid VV-ECMO capability.

strengths: Enrolled a clearly defined, very severe ARDS population.
Pragmatic network design including non-ECMO centres with retrieval.
Protocolised conventional management with explicit rescue ECMO criteria.
High adherence to allocated ECMO strategy (97.6% received ECMO).
limitations: Early stopping for futility with reduced sample size versus plan (249 vs 331 maximum).
Large attrition from eligibility to randomisation (249/1015), potentially limiting representativeness.
Composite “treatment failure” endpoint embeds crossover in the control definition.

critical_appraisal.summary: EOLIA is a well-conducted but inconclusive trial due to early stopping and high crossover; the point estimate suggests potential benefit, but the confidence interval crosses 1.0, and the open-label design introduces potential for bias in co-intervention use.
strengths: High protocol adherence in the intervention arm
weaknesses: Stopped early for futility, reducing power
High rate of rescue ECMO in the control group dilutes the treatment effect
Open-label design may influence co-intervention delivery

sections.authors_conclusion: EOLIA did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in 60-day mortality on the prespecified frequentist analysis, but the point estimate and secondary outcomes are compatible with clinically meaningful benefit in a subset of patients with very severe ARDS.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: EOLIA supports VV-ECMO as part of a structured escalation pathway (optimised conventional care plus rescue ECMO capability) for very severe ARDS, rather than as a mandatory early intervention for all.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with very severe ARDS (meeting EOLIA criteria) in experienced ECMO centres.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: ECMO is proven to reduce mortality in all severe ARDS; the primary endpoint was not statistically significant.
implementation_caveats: Requires a mature ECMO program with rapid cannulation capability.
Careful patient selection is critical, balancing potential benefit against a 46% risk of transfusion-requiring bleeding.
Optimal conventional care (including prone positioning) must be maximized before considering ECMO.

controversies.notes: Stopping for futility at 249 patients widened uncertainty, and the confidence interval remains consistent with meaningful mortality reduction; interpretation depends on philosophy of evidence thresholds and the weight given to rescue crossover.

controversies.topic: Crossover as dilution vs ethical necessity
controversies.notes: Rescue ECMO was frequent (28%) and associated with high mortality (57%), raising debates about whether earlier ECMO could be superior to delayed salvage in carefully selected patients.
A post hoc Bayesian analysis estimated a high posterior probability of mortality benefit across a range of priors, reframing EOLIA as “uncertain but likely beneficial” rather than “no effect”.

An individual patient data meta-analysis of CESAR and EOLIA reported lower 90-day mortality with ECMO (RR 0.75; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.94) and highlighted the extent of rescue ECMO in controls (17% overall; 35 in EOLIA).

Contemporary international guidelines recommend considering VV-ECMO in selected patients with severe ARDS at experienced centres, typically as escalation after evidence-based conventional strategies (including prone positioning).

context_related_trials.relation: An individual patient data meta-analysis of CESAR and EOLIA reported lower 90-day mortality with ECMO (RR 0.75; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.94).

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal timing for ECMO initiation in severe ARDS?
Can a subgroup of patients who benefit most from early ECMO be reliably identified at the bedside?
How can the significant bleeding risk associated with ECMO be mitigated?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For very severe ARDS, early VV-ECMO is a reasonable rescue strategy in experienced centers after optimizing conventional care, but it does not confer a proven mortality benefit and carries significant bleeding risk.
